text:
The Central Board of Secondary Education (CBSE) has not yet received a sanction order for paying Coempt Edu Teck, its vendor for a controversial on-screen marking system (OSM) that was marred by glitches after it was introduced in its 2026 board examinations for class 12. And, its finance section has no information on penalties imposed on the company.
This was revealed by the board in an October 14 reply to a Right to Information application filed by HT on August 22, five months after the board and the company faced scrutiny and criticism over student complaints of blurred answer sheets, mismatched copies and technical glitches before and after the Class 12 results were announced on May 13.
CBSE officials told HT in June, it would penalise Coempt EduTeck, for shortcomings in the online evaluation system.
In response to an RTI question on whether penalties have since been imposed on the company, CBSE’s finance department said: “No such information is available with the Finance Section.”
Responding to a question on whether CBSE had paid Coempt, the board said: “As per the records maintained in the Finance Division, no sanction order for payment towards the scanning of Class 12 examination answer books to any company/firm has been received in the Finance Division to date.”
CBSE, the education ministry and Coempt EduTeck did not respond to repeated attempts seeking comment for this story.
The August 2025 tender, on the basis of which Coempt was awarded the OSM contract, provided for financial penalties, including ₹ 1 lakh for every 15-minute delay in rectifying an issue flagged by CBSE. It also prescribed fines for delays in submitting root-cause analyses and providing technical support and training. However, on September 20, 2025, a corrigendum removed key references to blacklisting a vendor for such issues before Coempt was awarded the contract on December 5 that year.
Under the August 2025 tender, payment was to be calculated based on the actual number of Class 12 answer books scanned and uploaded, and was to be released after completion of all exam-related formalities, including results based on re-evaluated scripts, a CBSE official had told HT in June.

In an initial reply on September 28 to HT’s RTI application, CBSE said 11,37,560 answer books had been scanned and sent to students by 6pm on May 26, the extended deadline for such applications.
CBSE conducted its Class 12 examinations from February 17 to April 10 and declared the results on May 13; the pass percentage fell to 85.20% from 88.39% in 2025.
HT’s reporting has painted a picture of the OSM process rushed through without adequate preparation and training, with serious consequences for students. The rollout drew complaints over unexpectedly low marks when results were announced on May 13, and later students reported blurred scanned answer sheets, unchecked answers and discrepancies between marks awarded on individual pages and final totals during the re-evaluation process from May 19 onwards.
On June 2, the Centre transferred CBSE chairman Rahul Singh to the agriculture ministry and prematurely repatriated secretary Himanshu Gupta to his parent cadre, the Ministry of Home Affairs.
The Cabinet Secretariat on June 2 also constituted a one-member committee headed by S Radha Chauhan, chairperson of the Capacity Building Commission, to probe the procurement of OSM services. The panel was asked to submit its report to the Department of Personnel and Training (DoPT) within a month. On September 25, the Centre appointed Mandeep K Bhandari as CBSE chairperson, replacing Lokhande Prashant Sitaram and making Bhandari the third person to head the board in less than four months.
Sanjay Maurya is a Principal Correspondent with Hindustan Times, where he covers education, with a focus on school and higher education, competitive examinations, education policy and governance. Working as part of the National Bureau, he is based in New Delhi and reports on the Ministry of Education and covers various statutory bodies like UGC, AICTE and NCTE and autonomous bodies like CBSE and NCERT. His reporting also tracks the implementation of key government reforms and policies from school education to higher education including in IITs, NITs, IIMs, central and state universities, and their impact on students and educational institutions. His reporting on the irregularities and rushed implementation of CBSE's On-Screen Marking (OSM) system for evaluation of Class 12 board exams 2026, triggered administrative action, leading to the transfer of the board's two senior-most officials and the constitution of a committee to probe alleged irregularities in procurement process of the system. He joined Hindustan Times in December 2024. Prior to that, he had a three-year stint at Careers360, where he reported on school and higher education, entrance examinations, admissions, rankings and various education policies involving universities and professional education bodies. Over the years, Maurya has reported extensively on major developments in India's education sector, including the implementation of the National Education Policy (NEP) 2020, reforms in the National Testing Agency (NTA) following the NEET-UG 2024 controversy, changes in school education, higher education regulation, and the evolution of entrance examinations such as NEET, JEE and CUET. He regularly produces data-driven and explanatory stories based on government documents, parliamentary proceedings, court records and official data.
